utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, December 8th, 2009, and I greet our accused, the Defence counsel, all members of the OTP in this courtroom, as well as everyone helping us. Let me first give the floor to our Registrar, who has some IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Filip Filipovic. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC01144, and the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC01145. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Praljak is here in the courtroom, and I will read an oral decision which we were to render yesterday, but we decided to postpone it until today, since he wasn't in court yesterday. Oral decision on the behaviour of the accused Praljak during hearings. During the hearing of December 3rd, 2009, the accused Praljak once again took the floor in a totally uncontrolled and disproportionate fashion, thus hampering the correct course of the hearing. The Trial Chamber reminds the accused Praljak that in its order of November 17, 2009, on call to order, it had already warned the accused that his behaviour during hearings was unacceptable and that if such behaviour continued, the Trial Chamber would apply Rule 80 of the Rules. The Trial Chamber has noted that this warning did not prevent the accused Praljak from continuing to such attitude. The Trial Chamber thus informs the accused that next time he behaves in such fashion, it will, according to Rule 80(B) of the Rules, exclude him from the courtroom immediately. Very well. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you. I fully understand. There was no real intention on my part when I did what I did. I did not mean to demean the Trial Chamber or anything like that. I'm not trying to justify myself, but the reaction tells you that I'm still alive, that I'm still fully conscious and very emotional about everything that goes on here. It tells you that I'm a human being, one that is not ill-intentioned at all. I am what I am. Sometimes this causes me to jump into a torrent to save a person's life, into a wild torrent. I tried to get some rest, because I'm sure that I'm getting slightly too tense about some things here in this courtroom. I'll try to not do this again. Nevertheless, if it happens and if you punish me, I will accept your punishment for what it is. And that is as much as I can say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We took note of what you said. It is true that it is sometimes difficult to stay collected, and actually it happened to me three times already in this courtroom, once after an objection made by Mr. Karnavas, when I had asked a question regarding the meeting -- HVO meetings. Mr. Karnavas had raised an objection which I thought was totally out of proportion, but I tried to stay cool. Then another time, it was after something said by Mr. Scott, something that I really did not understand, and I also tried to -- I refrained myself. And the last time had to do with a translation problem. And there, again, I had really kept my cool. But you have to keep your cool and stay collected, and it's very difficult. But that's the rule of the game. You just have to stay cool. It's true that if we were in a procedure where things are easier for the accused and the lawyers, where the accused is next to his lawyer, so whenever there is a problem the accused can talk quietly to the lawyer in order to say what the problem is, it's easier, but you're very far from your lawyers and things are difficult. I believe that if yesterday Ms. Pinter and Mr. Kovacic had been next to you, this would not have happened, but that's not the way it is here. But we took due note of what you said. Please understand that the Judges have to make sure that the hearing runs smoothly. This is because of the Rules I have to do this. And if things get out of order, then they can use Rule 80 in order to control the proceedings. General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like the Chamber to please understand fully two things. Firstly, there is no ill intention at all on my part, when I act like that, to demean the Trial Chamber. Secondly, should I be punished, I would fully understand the need to protect the dignity of the Trial Chamber, and I would fully comply with any punishment that may or may not come my way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, two more things before we bring the witness into the courtroom. I would like to tell the Petkovic Defence that it already used 22 hours and 3 minutes. Our Registrar just told us that. That's the time elapsed so far. Secondly, Ms. Alaburic, when you can, please give us information on document 1D2664. I looked at it overnight. Actually, I scrutinised it overnight, and it seems that the words "Izetbegovic" or "president" is not in the document in B/C/S, nor in its English version. Of course, the important version is the B/C/S version, the original version. But here we have a gap, there's a void. This was a 207th session of the Presidency, and I would really like to know what happened. It started at 1.30 p.m. Does this mean that the meeting had already started during the morning, which might explain why there was another transcript for the morning and then they had a new transcript for the afternoon session, or maybe it's the person who actually transcribed the audiotape who forgot to mention the name of the speaker, i.e., Izetbegovic. Should it be Izetbegovic, of course. Or maybe this person did not understand who took the floor at the time. But I noted in the document that when the speaker is not identified, he is identified with an X. Maybe somebody decided to deliberately erase "Izetbegovic," but I would like to know whether this document was handed over by the OTP or whether you obtained it directly. I'm asking all these questions for a simple reason. I assume that in your IC lists, you're going to include this document, if it hasn't been admitted yet, and there will be objections raised, of course. And then we'll have a debate within the Bench. In order to make a decision, I absolutely need to have all this information, if you can provide it to me, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. What I can tell you about this document is as follows: This is a document proposed by the Prlic Defence, and it has been admitted already. We have been using it as such. It is a Prlic Defence document. I think it might be more appropriate for my learned friend Ms. Tomanovic to provide an explanation. I do have my view of these things, but I think she's probably better placed than I am to tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. If you look at the local version of this document, you have the ERN number, the Prosecution's ERN number in the upper right corner. We received the document in this condition from the OTP, and that is about as much as I can say. I can't say where the OTP got the document from. Nevertheless, we can ask around, work with the Prosecution to identify a source, and then we shall be better placed to answer your query.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it seems that this document comes from the OTP. You must have looked into this, because the opening sentence is a very important one. But maybe you know nothing about this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judge Trechsel, Judge Prandler, Judge Mindua. Good morning to all those in and around the courtroom. If you would allow me just one deviation for a moment, I'd like to introduce an intern who's been working with us who has not been in the courtroom before. This is Ms. Ophelia Claude. She is an intern who has been with us for some time and has not had the opportunity to sit in on a session and will joining us today and probably tomorrow, and I would like to present her to the Chamber. In response to your question, Your Honour, it is indeed from the OTP. It was part of the disclosures that we made, of course, sometime ago to all the Defence. We had made preliminary inquiries and had not yet obtained -- been able to find any additional information about that particular record. However, in light of the testimony over the last couple of days, we have re-initiated additional inquiries. I have no additional information to provide to the Chamber at this time, but we are pursuing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom. Of course, I agree to the new intern from the OTP, and I wish her the best for her internship with our Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask your permission for my assistant, Davor Lazic, to take a list of names through to the court reporter to avoid any problems over the course of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Can you hear the translation? I hope you can hear the translation. Could you please give us your last name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Bozo Peric, born on the 30th of June, 1954, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired. I retired as a brigadier of the Federation Army, but currently I don't do anything in particular for a living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you already testified in court or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time, but I did testify in Sarajevo at the Federal Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You testified in Sarajevo. Could you tell us in which case, regarding which accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maka Radic et al. I was a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you may sit down. Let me give you some information before we start. In order for this hearing to run smoothly, you've already testified in a court, so you will not be too surprised with the way this hearing will unfold. You will be answering questions put to you by Ms. Alaburic. I'm sure she already told you all this. She met with you, and she will deal with a number of issues that you have talked about, and she will show you documents that are in a binder. Then after her questions, the other Defence counsel, representing the other accused, might also put questions to you. Ms. Alaburic will use two hours for her examination-in-chief, and the Trial Chamber gave the other Defence teams one hour for questions. Then after this phase, Ms. West, the Prosecutor sitting on your right, will also put questions to you during her cross-examination. The four Judges on the Bench in front of you can intervene at any moment to put questions. Usually, they ask questions regarding the documents that are on the screen. You're a former serviceman, so I know that you will be very brief in your answers. Please be brief. If you do not understand the question put to you, just ask the person asking the question to reformulate it, even if it's a Judge. Even if you believe that the question is wrong or there's an error in the question, just say so, because you must absolutely answer, and your answer will be cast in stone. It will actually be transcribed on the screen in front of you in the transcript. You'll see that questions are put in different fashions. The Defence has a certain way of putting questions, the Judges have another way of putting questions, and the Prosecutor, Ms. West, will also put questions to you in a fashion that you might deem difficult, but that's the rule of the game. The Prosecutor can put questions to you by telling you what her position is, and then you can agree with it or not, but don't get all head up when you have questions by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor is doing his job. Sometimes there are court incidents because of the way the questions are put by the Prosecutor. The witnesses don't really understand the role played by the Prosecutor and the leeway that the procedure provides to the Prosecutor to put these kind of questions. So please listen carefully to the question and just answer. We break every hour and a half. You have made the solemn declaration, which means that you are now the witness of the Court. You are no longer to contact the Defence until your hearing is over, which should normally -- and this hearing should normally be over tomorrow, given the schedule. That's all I had to say. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Once again, good morning to everyone, my learned friends from the OTP, and in particular my learned friend Ms. West, whose examinations we always follow with particular attention. Good morning to the accused and to the witness, Mr. Peric, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try and start this off with some information on your life and work in order to better acquaint the Trial Chamber with your education and your career. You said you were born on the 30th of June, 1954?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Kuti Livac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You went to a school for electronics in Mostar. That was your secondary education; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then you got a job with the PTT, Post Telegraph Telephone, a state-run and state-owned company, where you stayed until 1984. 1984, that's right. In 1985, you set up a private telecommunications company. You designed telephone switch boards, telephone networks, and telephone lines, external ones; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How were you doing? How was your private business doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks for asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In October 1992, you arrived at the HVO Main Staff, where you took up the post of assistant chief for communications?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For wire communications; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In April 1994, you started working with the VOS at the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 1999, you went to work with the Defence Ministry of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Signals Department or the Communications Department. In 2001, you were retired, holding the rank of brigadier of the BH Federation Army. Mr. Peric, is all this information correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Peric, what were the components of the BH Federation Army, and how did that army come into existence?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Two components were united. One was the BH Army and the other one was the HVO. We used to refer to this as the H component and the B component when we spoke about it in shorthand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat this? And please try to speak a little more clearly, because the first letter was mis-recorded. How did you refer to these components?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Component H and component B.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the component H? That stood for the Croat component, and the B stood for the Bosniak; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak component. Up until about 1994, it used to be referred to as the Muslim component, and then the name was turned into the Bosniak component; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Around about that time, they started using their own name for their nation and started referring to themselves as Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, were your years of service with the HVO taken into account when your overall years of service were calculated in your new post?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, under the rules of retirement. The war, itself, up until the end of 1995, counted for double, and the rest is as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the same rule apply to the soldiers and officers of the BH Army, Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When, in October 1992, you came to the HVO Main Staff, how many people were working at the Main Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, we note the question of the pensions because it's been mentioned on several occasions, and you're not the first one talking about this, but let's be clear about this. You said that the years of service before 1995 counted for double. Does this mean that an HVO soldier - I'm talking about an HVO soldier - who was in an HVO unit, let's say an HVO brigade in 1993, does this mean that 1993 will count double for him, which means that when his pension will be computed, if he was in service in 1993, 1992 will count double? Is that the way it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I don't quite understand. When the war stopped, ended, each soldier who spent the war between 1992 and 1995 in active service had each of the years spent there counted for double, but only in relation to that period. But that's only for retirement purposes, whether one has enough years of service in order to retire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the case of an HVO soldier who was in the ranks of the HVO from 1992 to 1995. So 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995, four years altogether. Does this mean that when his pension was calculated, these four years counted for eight, for eight years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when he tabled his request for retirement, then. Then, in the retirement fund, his years of service are taken into consideration, and if he put in a request those four years he spent during the war he would count as double, he would get double credit, and this would count for eight years. So he could retire earlier than he would otherwise had those years not been counted as double.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, it's crystal clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, when, in October 1992, you arrived in the Main Staff, how many people were working there; in the Main Staff, that is?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: There were about 15 to 20 people. I don't think there were more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where was the Main Staff located, what premises?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It was located in a building which we referred to as the Agricultural Institute before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us what floor the Main Staff was on.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff was on the ground floor of that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did the building have several storeys?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which institution was on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the second floor?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think there was an accounts department and the SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Could the usher now help us out and hand this diagram over and place it on the ELMO. The diagram was drawn by Mr. Peric during the proofing session, and we also have copies for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Peric, let's try and describe these premises used by the Main Staff, although we have visited the building, but we didn't go inside the premises of the Main Staff, we went up to the first floor, when in 2006, June, we travelled to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now we can see the sketch, the diagram. Since this is in English, under number 1 is the office used by the chief of the Main Staff. Number 2 is the office of the chief of VOS and the other staff of the VOS. Room number 3 was the Communications Sector offices. So, Mr. Peric, you used office number 3, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Office number 4 was where the chiefs of the various sectors of the Main Staff were located. Number 5 was the Anti-Aircraft Defence, and there was a bed there, too, so that the person who had to spend the night there would have somewhere to sleep. Number 6 was the office in which the staff from the Operative and Training Department were located. Room number 7 was used by the secretary of the chief of the Main Staff, and room number 8 was the toilet. The staircase leading up to the first floor can also be seen. So tell us, Mr. Peric, is that what the building looked like on the ground floor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you sign that document now, please, and put today's date on it? And it's the 8th of December today. Have you got a pen?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document just signed by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC01146. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who was the communications -- what was the Communications Department made up of? Did it have any subsections?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was composed of -- well, there was the chief of communications, and he had his assistants for wire telecommunication, radio relay systems, and encryption.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the customary modus operandi. What would you do when you came in to work in the morning?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: We would come in in the morning at around 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you approach the microphone, please. You're very far away.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, I arrived at about 7.00 a.m., as did everybody else. We would sit down in that one room, one office. There was a communal table. The chief would be sitting at the head of the table, and we would sit around the table. We would have coffee or tea, and we would report, brief everybody about our work on the previous day. If there were any problems, or if a task wasn't carried out, or anything like that, we had to state the reasons for that, why we failed to carry out the assignment. And if there was some objective problems, then we would resolve them together. We would try and find the best way of solving the problem. After that, the chief would go off to a briefing, himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who did he go to see?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: To the Operations and Training Department. Who the person was there, I don't know, because I didn't go. I wasn't his deputy or anything. But I assume he went to see his superior and to brief him, or to attend a briefing. We waited for him to return, and during that time we would finish drinking coffee. We would wait for him to receive new instructions for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please --

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there duty shifts organised in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, and everybody had to do duty work from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So what was considered to be this duty time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That would be the time when the secretary went home, left the office, which means from 1600 hours to the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us now, was there a duty log-book of any kind?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a duty log-book in which the basic entries were recorded briefly. Information received by the duty officer during his shift would be recorded in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, during the shifts, did reports come in from the operations zones about the situation in those zones?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they came in orally, sometimes in written form, and then that went to the Operations and Training Department. And that department summarised all those reports into one report, one comprehensive report, which was then handed and sent over to the chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell us, Mr. Peric, in January 1993, after the representatives of the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina signed, in Geneva, the Vance-Owen peace agreement, peace plan, what was the atmosphere like in the Main Staff and in the environments in which you moved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you don't want to ask any more questions about duty shifts? Because if you don't, I do have some follow-up questions for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, that was not my intention, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, with this chart we can understand that you were in office number 3, that there was duty service only from 4.00 p.m. because that was the time when the secretary would leave. So the one who was on duty from that time on, from 4.00, where was he? In which office was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got the diagram before me, but the office where the chief of staff's secretary occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one on duty would be in office number 7, is that right, based on the diagram? And as I understand, this individual was there from 4.00 p.m. until the next morning, until such time as the secretary would arrive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What time did the secretary arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, she would be in the office by 8.00. Everybody would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And would there be people on duty on Saturdays, Sundays, on holidays? Let me take a specific example. Let us imagine that at 2.00 in the morning, a commander from the operative zone calls the person on duty. This call, will it arrive in office number 7 or in the communications office, in office number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 2.00 a.m., no commander would call up, as a rule. His duty officer would do that. Now, where the person is going to call depends where they're calling from, and that means that if they're calling from the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina, he will call up on the phone, one duty officer to another duty officer at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us imagine the case of Jablanica. Imagine there's a problem there at 2.00 a.m. and the head of staff has to be informed of it. Does the brigade commander in Jablanica or the duty officer call the duty officer located in office number 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you chose a good example, because the BH Army was in Jablanica, so they didn't call us up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take another location where the HVO was. You pick the example. Would the HVO brigade commander call the duty officer in office number 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's take the example of Tomislavgrad. The Military District of Tomislavgrad would act in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us imagine that this is about very important information. The duty officer in office number 7, can he straight away call the chief of staff, Mr. Petkovic or later on Mr. Praljak? Is there a direct chain of communication with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our duty log-books, we had the numbers -- the number of the mobile phone of the chief. It was written in the log-book. And that mobile phone wasn't like the mobile phones you have today. It was fixed to a vehicle, a car, and we had the fixed telephone number in the Logistics Centre in Grude, a land line in Grude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let us imagine that General Praljak, in August 1993, is asleep and something major happens. Can General Praljak be woken up straight away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you manage to reach him, then there would be no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say "if you manage to reach him." Were there cases when he could not be found, nor could General Petkovic be found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such cases, the duty officer in office number 7 finds out that there is nobody picking up in General Praljak's office, do you have a procedure to call somebody else then? It could be that General Praljak is somewhere else, is ill, or dead; you never know. Was there another procedure to call his assistant, somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there was. His assistant was there, who would stand in for him when he physically couldn't make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me dig a little deeper, because this is important. General Petkovic at times attended meetings in Geneva or elsewhere, so physically he was not in his office, office number 1. In such cases, as far as you can remember, was there someone standing in for General Petkovic or was it so that General Petkovic could be reached no matter where he was in the world, including in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Main Staff, if the chief was absent and there was something that he had to be told, the person informed was the chief of the Training Department, Training and Operations Department. I'm not sure if anyone could have got through to General Petkovic in Geneva. I certainly wasn't able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling us that if General Petkovic was somewhere else, it was, as a rule, the officer from the Training and Operation Department who was the one replacing him. But then within the Main Staff, as such, was there a document saying that the -- in the event that the chief of staff was absent, he would be replaced by the head of the Training and Operations Department, who, unless I'm mistaken, was Ivan Primorac at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about the Signals Department or the Communications Department, where I was. We had a head, and we had an assistant head who was also the deputy head. There were other assistants who were not his deputies. I suppose it worked like that in all the other departments too. Chief of the Main Staff, the chief had a deputy who was also the head of a certain department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I asked you about January 1993. The representatives of the Bosnian Croats signed the Vance-Owen Plan in Geneva. You, personally, and anyone else you knew at the Main Staff and elsewhere, how did you view the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the option of continuing to live side by side in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I thought it was done, the war had ended. It was time to start preparing for life returning to normal. I was assuming throughout that I would simply go back to my previous job. I was not a professional officer. I was what we call a newfangled officer. I thought I would continue in my old job, as most of my other friends who had jobs before the war. Very few of us, if any, had any serious intention of staying in the army for the rest of their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did remain in the Main Staff, after all, and unfortunately the war did not end. Let us see a number of documents about that. Let's look at the first one now. I suppose it's the first document in your folder. It's 4D1600. This is a list of persons who worked in the Main Staff. You see the names of the people occupying all the top posts in the Main Staff. We can see that General Praljak was commander. Mr. Peric, we see the Department of Communications and Encryption, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, did you not make a mistake? Because I can see in the transcript and also in French it is said that's the time when General Praljak was commander, but this document shows -- oh, yes, I see, the deputy was Mr. Petkovic. Sorry, sorry, you were right. The deputy was then Petkovic. Therefore, the commander was Mr. Praljak, but it's not stated as such in the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name is missing, where it says "Commander," but we know, because of everything that happened afterwards, Mr. Praljak was the commander. But we can ask the witness too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, are you the Bozo Peric here in this document?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we go to the very end of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, we understood, through Ms. Alaburic's question, that office number 1 was the office of the chief of staff. We also understood that Mr. Petkovic was chief of staff, and then he was replaced by General Praljak. Now, where was General Praljak's office and where was General Petkovic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we are talking about two different places. The ground plan that you were looking at a minute ago was about the Main Staff in Mostar, and what we're looking at now, the number you specified, that Main Staff was moved to Citluk, to an entirely different building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you see that it was a good idea to ask you that. Now, you drew up a map or a plan. That was when the Main Staff was in Mostar, so that was when General Petkovic was the chief of the Main Staff, but he was sent to Citluk. Can you tell us when, exactly; what month, what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They went to Citluk in 1993. I think it was in September or October 1993, but I can't be certain for quite another reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're now bringing in a problem. From what we know, General Praljak took office officially on the 27th of July, 1993, which means that on the 27th of July, 1993, he must have sat down in office number 1, if, as you say, the Main Staff was moved to Citluk in September. If it is so, then where did Mr. Petkovic sort of settle in in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may assist. This ground plan states the exact time until which the Main Staff remained in that building, and that also is the date when the Main Staff moved to Citluk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, does this mean that the Main Staff moved in July?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic is saying that the move was on July 18th, 1993. Why didn't you draw the ground plan of the Main Staff in Citluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one ever asked. I'm not a construction expert by profession, and I don't think I would be able to draw a ground plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But when you were in Citluk, did you have an office? Did the Communications Centre have an office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that most of the departments were in a large -- well, not really a basement; more like the ground floor of that building. And then the offices had partitions dividing them, all of them with a -- in practical terms, and there was always a corner that one could withdraw to for some silence and quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, neither I nor any members of my team are construction experts, but we like to do ground plans, and we'd love to do a ground plan of the Citluk building for you. Nevertheless, this witness is here only for the purpose of everything that happened up until the 30th of June, 1993, that being the reason why we don't have any ground plans for these later buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, may we now go back to the list of persons who worked for the Main Staff at the time. If you look at the names who were working there at the time, can you tell us, more specifically, which month this list might be in relation to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: This is a list that came about when I came back to Citluk. I think it might have been around the 1st of September. These persons probably filled some posts in the Main Staff, all of which had gone on while I was away because I had a duty to discharge elsewhere. I returned to the staff sometime around October, mid-September or October. I'm looking at the names of these persons, and some of these persons, not all by any means, but some, had been appointed before I returned; for example, Ivica Tutsa [phoen] from my department, I find him there, and then when I left to work elsewhere -- when I first left, he wasn't there yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you returned to the Main Staff. You were an employee or an officer of the Main Staff throughout, as a matter of fact; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But for a while you had work to do elsewhere, specifically Sector North in Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at the information towards the end of this overview, we see that the total number of persons working there was 114 under the establishment; 43 per cent Main Staff, or, rather, the replenishment levels in the Main Staff -- the manning levels were 43 per cent, 51 persons working there, and it says without the command itself, 37 persons working there. Mr. Peric, the Command Centre, what exactly do they mean by the Command Centre?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: A group of people who are providing for the technical needs of the Main Staff, supplying all sorts of equipment that was required and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just -- Your Honours, if I may just correct one thing. "The Command Centre," I don't think that is a good interpretation. It might cause some confusion. The command -- "domiza povatnistva" [phoen] is an auxiliary service, general-purpose clerks, janitors, cleaning ladies, drivers. I don't think it should be called the Command Centre, but I really don't know what we should call it. I think "Housekeeping," "Command Housekeeping," would be a good idea, or some sort of service here. General Praljak is suggesting that we use the word "service." I think that would be the best option. I'm sorry for needing to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I find it difficult to follow. Ms. Alaburic told us that you would testify on the period before June 30th, but the document we have here represents the Citluk Main Staff which was set up as of July 18th. Now, regarding the figures, we see that there were 114 people altogether. That was the establishment. But, in fact, there was only 51 people working there. Early in the morning, when you started testifying, you told us that Main Staff in Mostar, there were 15 to 20 people only, and now I have a document which shows that there were five times more people. So why is it that the manpower was multiplied by almost five when the Main Staff moved from Mostar to Grude -- I mean, to Citluk? Sorry. Is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a perfectly logical explanation. First of all, the number has doubled or maybe been multiplied by a factor of 2.5, perhaps even less. You see the number of officers. Under the establishment book, that is how many officers should have been there. Furthermore, you have the number of officers who were actually there, which is over 50 per cent fewer officers than there should have been. Why were between 15 and 20 of them in Mostar? Well, I think for two reasons, but this is just my opinion. I'm not stating a fact here. The area in Mostar was quite a lot smaller, the other reason being this: the other reason being at the time we didn't have too many properly-trained professional officers. The few that we did have and the few that we could use to fill posts in the Main Staff we would normally dispatch to operations zones because those were the most important areas during the clashes against the VRS. We believed it was a better idea to have our operations zones filled properly, manned properly, rather than the Main Staff itself. With the departure to Citluk, the area was enlarged, and so the number of staff increased, too, but that's my opinion. I didn't read that anywhere, but I consider that that is roughly how things were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, since you're giving us your opinion about the increase in staff members in the Main Staff compared to October 1992 and that period, let me ask this: In your opinion, was it a fact that the conflict with the BH Army was something that the HVO did not expect to see in 1992, and that with the development of the war -- all right, I'll rephrase that question. Tell us, Mr. Peric, in your opinion, the war situation during 1993, was it different compared to what it was like in 1992 or could they be said to be roughly the same?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, they couldn't be said to be the same at all. I said a moment ago that at the beginning of 1993, I and many of my friends and associates were thinking about civilian life in Bosnia in the various civilian sectors of life after the war. It was only later on that we realised that the war had, in fact, just begun.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, if you happen to remember, whether with the complex war situation that developed, that there were more and more people in the Main Staff, or was there no correlation between the number of people and the strength of the Main Staff and the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I think while we had the conflict in 1992 and the beginning of 1993, during that period, the Main Staff could perform its functions fairly well. However, once the conflict with the BH Army broke out, well, I'm not the right person to make an assessment about that, I suppose, but probably there was more work, requiring greater involvement and more manpower.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Peric, take a look at the next document, please, which is 4D324, and it is an information put out by Arif Pasalic to the Main Staff and the Mostar Operation Zone. And in this document, in point 3, it says that the line of separation has been agreed upon at Bijela Bridge, Drenovac Ravine, and Povezak. And then in point 4, it says that the 2nd Brigade will lay a telephone cable connecting the units of the BH Army to the command post of the 4th Battalion of the BH Army. Tell us, please, Mr. Peric, do you have any knowledge about this laying of a telephone cable?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Because this area is a region where I come from, so the communications chiefs in the brigade or battalion knew me very well, and they asked me to help them procure about 10 kilometres of this PTK cable. And you see that that is what is written in brackets, "PTK field telephone cable." And as far as I remember, I managed to find 8 kilometres of this PTK cable, but that seemed to suffice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, from this document it would follow that on the 12th of April, 1993, which is a very important date for us, the HVO was laying telephone cables for the units of the BH Army to link up with the Command of the BH Army; is that what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can conclude that from what it says here. I wasn't on the site, myself, and I wasn't involved in laying the cables. I just procured the cables and means for them to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Kim West for the Office of the Prosecution. The last question, again, is a very leading question. I would just ask counsel to refine the form of her questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, please put neutral questions to the witness and let him answer. Don't prompt the answers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't agree that it's a leading question this time, because I was reading the contents of this document, and then, after having read them, I asked whether that was actually what happened. Did the HVO lay telephone cables linking a unit of the BH Army with the Command of the BH Army? So my question to the witness was, Did this actually happen? And the witness answered the question. Now, I have another question when we're talking about these events in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At this time, and we're dealing with April 1993 -- up until that time, did a shell fall on Mostar, East or West, from the positions of the Bosnia and Herzegovinian Serbs at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Very, very often, both on Mostar and the broader area around Mostar, including, for example, my own village, the place I'm from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Peric, what place is that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I have two answers. One is the village, itself, Kuti Livac, and the area around it which is referred to and called Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me return to these 8 PTK kilometres. I'm interested in that. You told us that these telephone lines were laid in order to make sure that there could be communication between the BH Army and the HVO; is that it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's to make sure that the HVO and the BH Army could communicate; is that it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if need be, I will clarify that, but it's sufficient to say that they set out communication points in the Command of the BH Army and the HVO. Now, whether they lifted the receiver to sing songs to each other or to convey something else, I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are saying that there was a device that existed to make sure that the two sides could communicate. The question that Ms. Alaburic should have put to you, and I'm going to put to you, is why such a link was set up. Why did people believe it was necessary to place a communication line between the BH Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because those two units joined at that point, and they had to have communication amongst themselves and with their commands. So we're talking about a small NATO system, when you have two armies, two commands, a joint command which commands both these two commands, subordinated to them -- to it. That's why they needed the cable, to convey the orders and not to be intercepted on the radio relay connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you anticipated my next question, but I'll still put it to you. When this kind of technical operation is carried out, is it done between friendly armies or enemy armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between allies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I give you an example in history and there are many that I could use, but I'll pick one. In Stalingrad, I don't think that the Russian Army was linked to the German Army. I don't think they had set up a communication line in order to communicate; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think they did either, but I'm not sure. Perhaps they did. Who knows?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do thank you for your questions, because they made me look at the entire text in English, and I see that it wasn't an integral one. My questions related to a part of item 4 which talks about laying down a cable from the units of the BH Army to the Command of the BH Army, and now I see that in the English text, after the word "4th Battalion," it doesn't say that it's the BH Army, so I'd like to go back to the document and summarise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, when we look at this portion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic. I had also been misled, perhaps, perhaps. But the 2nd Brigade here, that is the HVO 2nd Brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's try, Mr. Peric, to clarify this. Looking at the original language, B/C/S, who is doing the laying of the telephone cables, who's laying the telephone cables?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Soldiers are laying the cable who are in the Communications Section of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Of which army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: In this case, the 2nd Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to correct my question in line 25. I did not ask in which area. I asked in which army. And the witness said the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the HVO brigade is laying down cables. Let's see where it's laying them down from. It says: "From the command post of the battalion commander to the BH Army units at Bijela." Tell us, please, Mr. Peric, which armies, by laying down this cable, are being linked?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, the 2nd Brigade, which is made up of battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Of which army, though?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The HVO. The 2nd Brigade of the HVO is being linked up with a military unit of the BH Army at Bijela Bridge. They are laying cables down to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's see where the cables are being laid down further. So from this unit of the BH Army, from the BH Army unit at Bijela Bridge, they are laying a cable to the Command Post of the 4th Battalion of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this second laying of cables, within whose army is that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Within the BH Army, and they're being laid -- the cable is being laid that are in the Communications Department of the BH Army. I don't see what is being challenged or is contentious there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I think we've clarified the situation, Your Honours, and we can move on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this means that the Command of the 2nd Brigade and the Command of the 4th Battalion of the BH Army could communicate through this cable; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I just draw your attention to something here? The 2nd Brigade appears very often here, is mentioned often here, without HVO. That's because the HVO took over the terminology of NATO, and the BH Army retains the terms used in the JNA. So there it's "battalion," "company." With us it's -- with the HVO, a company is "satnija," a battalion is "bojna," but I'm sure that somebody has already explained all that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on to another document, could you look at paragraph 4 in the B/C/S, where Mr. Pasalic is explaining why there is a need to lay this cable. He says that it is to have co-ordination among forces and to defend the area. Was that the motivation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm now moving on to another area, the 9th of May, 1993, and I think it would be a good idea to take the break now. I apologise, but I'd just like to -- my colleague has drawn my attention to the fact that the witness's answer to you, Judge Antonetti, was not recorded. Could you repeat your answer, please, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said a lot. It was a long answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said "precisely," I believe.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, "precisely."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I asked you to take a look at paragraph 4, where Mr. Pasalic is explaining why there was a need to lay this cable, and he says it's for co-ordination between the forces and to defend the sector. I asked you whether that was the motivation behind the laying of the cable. What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that was precisely the reason. I said "precisely." I didn't say "the reason," I just said "precisely."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your answer is now on the transcript. I trust everyone helping us here, I don't check things, and it's a good thing that the lawyers are checking everything, because your answer was not noted on the transcript. I don't have my eyes, you know, on the transcript. I'd rather look at the witness. But now let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, before we start talking about the 9th of May, 1993, there is one clarification that I will be needing from you. When you were asked by Judge Antonetti -- I'll just dwell on General Petkovic for the moment. Say you are the duty officer. Did you have any information as to what the right telephone numbers were to reach Petkovic, as chief of the Main Staff? You say you had his mobile phone, and you say you could also call the operations duty officer in Grude?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This operation duty officer in Grude, why is he important, in terms of your duty roster and in terms of your ability to reach General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Because the general would sometimes sleep in Grude, he would spend the night there, and the operations duty officer at the Logistics Centre probably knew his whereabouts. I didn't know the exact building in which he slept, and he probably did. I didn't know the extension for that particular building, and I don't think any of the other duty officers knew; at least officially they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So let's suppose that General Petkovic was not in his vehicle and you were unable to reach him on his mobile phone that was stationary in his car. You would call the duty operations officer in Grude, and then he would try to track down General Petkovic somewhere in Grude; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: We'd call the duty officer. We'd tell him that we needed to speak to General Petkovic. He'd say, All right, if he's around, I'll let him know. That sort of thing. The duty officer says he's not around, then we ask him to try and track him down and please ask him to get back in touch. Why should he get in touch? Because we have no idea how much time it will take him to track him down for him to call us back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's assume General Petkovic is not sleeping in Grude. Let's say he's off to see his family in Split or is elsewhere; for example, in Kiseljak. In your duty register, is that actually indicated, that he would be spending that day in Kiseljak or in Split? Is that something you'd be aware of?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: If he's away somewhere on business, the chief, he normally informs us where he's off to. If it's a private matter, we normally have nothing to do with it and remain in the dark. This is the sort of information that he would be leaving with the Grude Logistics Centre in case he was off on some sort of private business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. Thank you, Ms. Alaburic, for asking the question, because earlier on I was a bit in the dark. When we were looking at the building of the Main Staff with the seven offices in it, I wondered where the duty operation officer was, because I kept in mind that in modern armies, everything is sort of located together at the Main Staff and there's always somebody with the maps in front of him who receives faxes and telex messages and encrypted messages, and here I find out that there was also an operation officer in Grude. That's what you say. So this duty operation officer in Grude, in which building was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a former factory. It used to be a factory before the war. I think it was a plastic factory which stopped operating at the beginning of the war, and the factory itself and the administrative buildings were now used as a logistics base. The duty officer was there. I'm not sure which office exactly he occupied. But they did have a duty officer. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a theoretical case. Let us imagine that Colonel Blaskic, the commander of the operative zone, sends an encrypted report with mention saying "Urgent." As I understand it, this encrypted message may arrive, let's say, at 3.00 a.m., and it arrives in office number 3, if all goes well, and it is then decoded. Now, how do you make the connection from there with the duty operation officer in Grude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably that we weren't sufficiently clear, or perhaps I wasn't. The messages would arrive in a different building that was close to the other building housing the Main Staff. The packet radio equipment was in that building, too, and that is normally where reports from all of our operations zones would arrive. The packet radio equipment operated around the clock. It would receive and decode all sorts of incoming messages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you see it was a good idea to ask these questions, because we do find things out. You say that packet messages would not arrive in office number 3. They would go to another building where they were processed. Now, what about this other building? Was it also a Main Staff building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That building was not used by the Main Staff, but there was a part of that building where we had the packet radio equipment, as we called it. I explained about who was working in the Communications Department. I said there was a person in charge of encryption. This is precisely something that was part of his work. His communication was precisely about that. There was this room where we kept the packet radio equipment, and he was supposed to communicate with everyone. He was supposed to decode any incoming message and then forward it depending on who it was addressed to. None of the messages reached office number 3. I think the head of the Communications Department was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the building where the packet messages would get, where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite near the building housing the Main Staff, the distance between the two being no more than 20 metres, give or take a metre or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I'm trying to reconstruct it all, but it is extremely complicated. I learn now that there was the building on the ground floor with the seven offices, where there's a duty service and where the secretary arrives in the morning and leaves at 4.00. So there's a duty service operating there. And there's office number 3, where you were, where you would decode messages, among other things. And then 20 metres from there, there's another building where all the radio communication gets to. And then in Grude, we have the duty officer who's located in that former factory. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe you misunderstood, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then make it clear for me, because I'm really trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I was quite clear about office number 3. There was nothing that was being decoded there, no incoming mail at all. It was an office that we used, but there was the other building at a distance of about 20 metres from this building, and there was another room there, about 15 or 16 square metres, where we kept the packet radio equipment. There were persons there who were there around the clock receiving all the incoming communication. The encryption and the decoding of any messages was done there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood as much, but I seem to understand something else, and I stand to be corrected, of course. But when General Petkovic takes the stand, he will be able to explain it all to us. But as I understand it, whenever something happens somewhere, the commander of the operative zone sends an encrypted report that will get to a building -- will arrive in a building that is 20 metres from your building, and that is where the encrypted message is decoded. Your own service is located on the ground floor of the building, where there's a duty service and where you can call the chief of the Main Staff. And then in Grude, there's the operations officer who's located in the factory. So is this the way it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said it just right, but I don't see any connection between there being an operations duty officer in Grude and the decoding process for these messages. I'm not sure why you seem to be somehow linking these two or what the context is or the need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a question. I'll answer it. Let us imagine that something happened, there is a really extraordinary event that takes place. This is in theory. Let us suppose that the BH Army is attacking and the HVO is losing the battle, so general panic and disorder prevails. Let us imagine that Colonel Blaskic sends a very sensitive report to say that, Our lines have been broken, we are now fleeing. All this is being encrypted. So in this case, this message would reach the building that is 20 metres from yours, and there it would be decoded. And I suppose that the operations officer in Grude would be informed of it straight away. You see, that's the link I'm trying to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, by no means. Let's do it this way: Let's say your hypothetical case occurs, which is very much like reality. Then the decoded message would not be forwarded to Grude. It would go to whoever it was addressed to. Was it the chief of the Main Staff? In that case, it would go straight to the chief of the Main Staff. If the chief of the Main Staff was away and we were unable to trace him on his mobile phone or the one that he kept in his car, then we would go to the duty operations officer in Grude. We'd ask for him to try and get in touch with General Petkovic and whether he knew his whereabouts. That was the extent of the role of the duty officer in Grude, to check whether he knew where he was and to see if he could perhaps track him down, and to send the message through to him to get back in touch with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To go back to my example, I think I'm starting to understand. Back to my example. Colonel Blaskic would send his report to the chief of staff, and the report would have reached straight away the duty operation officer in Grude; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you these questions. I'm trying to understand how information is forwarded from the field to the chief of staff. I'm trying to find out how the chief of staff is informed of an event that is taking place on the ground. I'm trying to understand how the information circulates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to explain. You understood everything, you got it all right, except you don't go to the Logistics Centre in Grude, because in 99 per cent of the cases the chief is there. The remaining 1 or 2 per cent of cases are the moments when he's physically away, and in such cases, very rare ones, we talked to the man in Grude to see if he knew where General Petkovic was. He receives a transcript or a decoded message. He doesn't know about this, nor indeed does he know why we want to speak to the general. We simply talk to him to see if he can trace the general, in case he's anywhere in Grude. If he's not, he's bound to tell us, I don't know, either. I have no idea where he is, and I can't track him down. You understood everything up to the moment where you start asking, Why does the message go through to the duty officer in Grude? It actually doesn't, and he never gets to he see it, and he doesn't know that it's there. He doesn't know the message has arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure how it was interpreted into French because I've been monitoring the transcript. I'm quite sure there's a misunderstanding there. Page 43, line 21 and line 22, the witness says about the duty officer in Grude, and he says he does not receive a decoded message, he does not know what the message says, and the transcript states that he does know. That may be a source of the misunderstanding, and maybe even previously, although I must say I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So we understand that the duty officer in Grude does not know the contents of the encrypted message because the latter is going to arrive in the building that is at a distance of 20 metres in relation to yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It arrives there because that is where the packet radio equipment is. The packet radio equipment is in that building that is 20 metres away from our building, the Main Staff building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is extremely complicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let's try and clarify things. This duty officer in Grude, he wasn't a member of the Main Staff, or was he?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No. The Logistics Centre does not belong to the Main Staff, establishment-wise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in that Logistics Centre in Grude, were duty shifts organised around the clock, 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, around the clock. Who was on duty, I don't know, and how this was organised, I don't know, but you could reach them at a given telephone number 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Except for this Logistics Centre in Grude, was there some other daily shift in Grude or was the Logistics Base the only sure place where you would always find someone on duty?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I know about the Logistics Base. There's always someone there. Now, for other institutions, I don't know. Probably the police have a round-the-clock duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, when did you try to reach someone through the Logistics Base in Grude if you couldn't reach them directly on their mobile phone or land line?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, usually we would ask whether General Petkovic was there. When it was indispensable that he be informed, then we tried to reach him in that way. And if we can't reach him in that way, then we try and reach him in a hundred other ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, tell us, why were you trying to reach General Petkovic precisely in Grude?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Because the general often spent the night in Grude. I don't know in which building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if General Petkovic had decided to spend the night in Medjugorje, for example, and if you knew about that, would you then call the Logistics Centre in Grude at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, no way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Judge Antonetti, whether the situation is a bit clearer to you now and the position of this Logistics Centre in Grude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one follow-up question. As to this Logistics Centre in Grude, is that part or under the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was like this: It belongs -- it is under the auspices of --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we secure the witness's seat, because it's wobbly, so can we do something to keep the backrest in an upright position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take another chair. Witness, I'm going to ask my question again about the Logistics Centre in Grude. I asked you whether it was part of or under the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it comes under the Ministry of Defence, or the Department of Defence, as you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Peric, when this duty officer in Grude goes off to fetch General Petkovic, who's in Grude then, what does this duty officer in Grude -- what can this duty officer in Grude tell General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, he can tell him that he was called up by the Main Staff and that he should call them back, call the Main Staff back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, okay. I think that is a good foundation for our discussion next. Now, I'm going to begin with the 8th of May, 1993. So could you please tell me, what was the working day like at the Main Staff? Did anything happen that was different to the previous days? Were there any different, unusual messages coming in, or a lot of commotion, or whatever? Describe that day to us.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll describe it to the best of my recollections. I'll try and give you some details, too, if I can remember. Anyway, on the 8th it was just like any other day. Nothing indicated that something special was happening. We were given our regular assignments, and I was on duty from 4.00 onwards. Nobody liked doing duty work much, so that was the only slightly unusual thing compared to other days.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when you started your duty shifts, did you move to the office where the secretary of the chief of the Main Staff usually sat?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to her, and she briefly told me -- conveyed the daily messages that I should send out to someone, or with respect to the general's stay, whether he was there or not, whether we could reach him in Grude or not. Anyway, she would orally impart this information to us. Now, through the duty log-book, the duty roster, this would be recorded in writing. An entry would be made as to what we should pay attention to, what I should pay attention to during my shift, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on that particular day, in the log-book was there an entry about General Petkovic's movements at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was recorded and conveyed to me in the way in which I have described. It said that General Petkovic, with the minister, would tour the Military District of Tomislavgrad. Of course, the telephone numbers would be recorded, too, where they could be reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you said "with the minister." Now, at that time there was still no ministers. They were representatives of departments. But tell us which department in particular here. Which did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
